newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Odds favour broader EMU membership in 1999.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Odds favour broader EMU membership in 1999.

text.p: Expectations of a broader membership for European monetary union in 1999 have risen sharply because of recent events in France and Germany, a Reuters survey showed on Wednesday.

In a monthly survey of European economic and monetary union (EMU) expectations, 21 out of 47 contributors, or 45 percent, said they expected Italy would be included in the first wave, if it goes ahead in January 1999, compared with 14 percent last month.

Seventy-two percent and 77 percent of the political analysts, academics and economists who contributed to the poll said they expected Portugal and Spain respectively to be in from the start, up from 53 percent and 55 percent in May's survey.

These EMU "also-rans" have gained popularity because recent events have highlighted the problems France and Germany are facing to meet the stringent economic targets for membership, analysts contributing to the poll said.

In particular, they said it was unlikely the two EMU superpowers would be able to meet the budget deficit targets for 1997 contained in the Maastricht treaty. And if the entry rules had to be bent for France and Germany, other countries would demand similar treatment, the analysts said.

"If the problems in meeting the public deficit criteria in Germany and France accelerate, any arguments to exclude Italy will be limited," said Peter Brezinchek, chief analyst at Raiffeisen Zentralbank in Austria.
"(But) Portugal and Spain will be allowed in because they are on track to meet the criteria," he said.

The survey was carried out between June 6 and 9 as France's newly-elected Socialist government sent shockwaves through the European Union by asking to reflect further on a key element of EMU designed to promote the stability of the euro.

In the poll, contributors forecast on average a 76 percent likelihood that EMU would start on time in 1999. This compares with 82 percent in the survey a month ago and 72 percent on June 2, the day after the election which brought the French Socialists to power.
The Reuters poll showed that the lira, the peseta and the escudo were the currencies which would decide the euro's reputation as a "hard" or "soft" currency.
Of those who responded, 98 percent said the inclusion of the Italian lira would mean a weaker euro.
Sixty percent and 64 percent said the Portuguese escudo and Spanish peseta would have to be excluded from the single currency club for the euro to be rated as hard.

"They have all improved in inflation terms, but it is still high in comparison to other countries in the European Union (EU)," said Marc Touati, economist at Caisse Centrale des Banques Populaires in Paris.
"Historically all three have weak and volatile currencies," said Touati.
Michael Lewis, senior European economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London, expects Spain and Portugal to be allowed in at the launch of the single currency, but not Italy.
"Our concern is that Germany will find it difficult to sell the single currency domestically, if it includes the lira, at least in the first wave," he said.
"It is almost impossible for Germany to make the three percent target, but we are not giving up hope yet."
Twenty-seven of those surveyed said they expected Germany to meet the budget deficit criteria. Seventeen said they did not believe there was any way to make up the shortfall.
"We're scraping the barrel, but they may come through with spending freezes, higher taxes and privatisation revenues to make up the shortfall," said Lewis.

Some contributors suggested that creative accounting and a flexible interpretation of the Maastricht criteria may be the only way Germany can bring its budget deficit to or below three percent of gross domestic product(GDP) in 1997 and ensure a timely EMU start.

Germany's problems in meeting the public deficit criteria were highlighted last month when the government attempted to revalue Bundesbank gold and dollar reserves in a bid to meet the Maastricht budget deficit and public debt targets.
In France, pre-election promises, mainly regarding employment, are hampering attempts to meet the Maastricht gauge.
French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin said on Monday he wanted to renegotiate the stability pact to take account of important factors such as unemployment, which in April was at a record 12.8 percent.
